derivation_notes: The parent assumed substrate binding leaves the catalytic protonation equilibria unchanged. Here substrate occupancy S/(K_M + S) shifts the apparent protonation balance of the productive configuration, so the protonation terms become a nested nonlinear function of both pH and substrate occupancy; the parent is recovered when delta_pKa_coupling = 0.
change_summary: Relaxed the separability assumption between substrate binding and protonation by allowing substrate occupancy to bias apparent catalytic-group pKa values. This creates a genuine pH-by-S interaction, so the normalized pH-rate profile can change with substrate concentration.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The productive protonation fraction is identical for free and substrate-bound enzyme, so substrate binding does not shift the apparent catalytic-group pKa values.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Binding of substrate in the active site can electrostatically or conformationally stabilize one catalytic protonation state over another, causing substrate-dependent apparent pKa shifts and therefore substrate-dependent pH-rate profiles.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: Set delta_pKa_coupling = 0 to recover the parent expression exactly.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed enzyme parameters, pH only scales the Michaelis-Menten rate through a substrate-independent productive-fraction term 1/(1 + 10**(pKa_low - pH) + 10**(pH - pKa_high)), so changing S alters only the usual saturation factor and cannot shift the apparent pH optimum or pH-profile width.
response_change.child_relation: Allow substrate binding to perturb the protonation equilibrium of the productive catalytic configuration, so the pH dependence of activity changes with S; equivalently, the apparent pKa balance or productive occupancy becomes substrate-dependent, creating a non-separable pH-by-S interaction in the rate law.
response_change.observable_effect: When pH is scanned at multiple substrate concentrations with temperature and ionic strength fixed, the child can show a substrate-dependent shift or asymmetry of the activity-pH peak, whereas the parent predicts the same normalized pH profile at all S.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Most visible when substrate occupancy is appreciable, S on the order of K_M or larger, and when pH is sampled near either flank of the activity bell where small pKa shifts measurably change the rate; negligible in the low-substrate limit S << K_M.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: Within training, different S values already change rate amplitude; with the refinement they also change pH-profile shape or peak location. In holdout at higher or intermediate S, this same coupling becomes clearer because occupancy-dependent protonation bias grows smoothly with S.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent when substrate binding does not alter protonation energetics, e.g. the coupling parameter tends to zero so the productive-state fraction becomes independent of S.
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Binding of substrate in the active site can electrostatically or conformationally stabilize one catalytic protonation state over another, causing substrate-dependent apparent pKa shifts and therefore substrate-dependent pH-rate profiles.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is structurally harder than a coefficient-only correction because substrate occupancy is first combined with S through S/(K_M + S) and then inserted inside the exponents that govern the protonation nonlinearities, changing pH-profile shape rather than only global gain.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: The productive protonation fraction is identical for free and substrate-bound enzyme, so substrate binding does not shift the apparent catalytic-group pKa values.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: Substrate occupancy biases the apparent protonation equilibria of the productive catalytic configuration through an occupancy-dependent pKa shift.
evolution_contract.after_fragment: k_cat*E_total*S/((K_M + S)*(1 + 10**(pKa_low - pH - delta_pKa_coupling*S/(K_M + S)) + 10**(pH - pKa_high - delta_pKa_coupling*S/(K_M + S))))
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Parent response relationship: with pH varied and S varied independently while temperature and ionic strength are held fixed, v_pH factorizes into a saturation term S/(K_M+S) times a single shared bell-shaped pH activity factor. Child change: the occupancy-dependent shift delta_pKa_coupling*S/(K_M + S) alters the slopes and curvature of the bell through the protonation exponents, so increasing S can move the apparent optimum and change flank asymmetry or width. This changed target mapping is observable when comparing pH scans across substrate concentrations, especially for S ~ K_M or larger and near the bell flanks; it is weak in the low-substrate limit S << K_M.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this contrast because the parent enforces exact separability: after normalization by S/(K_M+S), the pH profile is independent of S by construction. Refitting k_cat, K_M, pKa_low, and pKa_high once for all conditions can rescale amplitude or choose one common bell shape, but it cannot make the pH optimum or profile width shift systematically with S.

evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current law assumes protonation equilibria are unaffected by substrate occupancy, making the pH modulation fully separable from substrate dependence except for an overall Michaelis-Menten factor.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: The productive protonation fraction is identical for free and substrate-bound enzyme, so substrate binding does not shift the apparent catalytic-group pKa values.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Binding of substrate in the active site can electrostatically or conformationally stabilize one catalytic protonation state over another, causing substrate-dependent apparent pKa shifts and therefore substrate-dependent pH-rate profiles.
evolution_plan.rationale: Parent response relationship: with pH varied and S varied independently while temperature and ionic strength are held fixed, v_pH factorizes into a saturation term S/(K_M+S) times a single shared bell-shaped pH activity factor. Thus the parent enforces the same normalized pH curve for all substrate concentrations and only changes amplitude with S. A realistic next refinement is to relax that separability by allowing substrate binding to bias catalytic-group protonation. Then the child's target mapping changes, not merely an auxiliary quantity: at moderate to high S, the pH optimum and/or flank steepness can differ from those at low S. This is scientifically admissible for enzymes whose bound substrate perturbs local electrostatics, and it is observable under the stated protocol because pH and S are both sampled directly. A single refit of all parent parameters cannot reproduce a substrate-dependent shift in the pH peak or width across S, because in the parent pH-profile shape is independent of S by construction. The effect can be weak or absent for some enzymes, and it may be hard to detect if all sampled S are far below K_M or if the coupling is intrinsically tiny; in that limit the parent remains an adequate approximation.

derivation_notes: The parent assumes ideal unit-slope protonation equilibria for both activity-limiting ionizations. Here the alkaline inactivation branch is refined to a non-ideal apparent Hill-like proton dependence, consistent with microscopic heterogeneity or coupled proton linkage while preserving rapid equilibrium and the same substrate-dependent pKa shift.
change_summary: The alkaline inactive branch now competes with the productive branch with adjustable pH steepness instead of a fixed unit log-slope. This changes the curvature and asymmetry of the pH-rate profile at fixed substrate concentration while reducing exactly to the parent when n_high = 1.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: Macroscopic protonation equilibria behave ideally, so each inactive/productive partition contributes as a simple 10^(±(pH-pKa)) term with exponent 1.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Microscopic heterogeneity or coupled proton linkage makes the alkaline inactivation transition non-ideal, yielding an effective Hill-like proton dependence for loss of activity on the high-pH flank.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: Setting n_high = 1 recovers the parent expression exactly.

response_change.parent_relation: The productive fraction is controlled by two unit-slope protonation transitions in log10 space, so the pH-rate profile has a fixed bell-shape sharpness at each substrate level; substrate only translates the apparent pKa boundaries together through the same occupancy-dependent shift.
response_change.child_relation: Allow one protonation transition, most naturally the alkaline inactivation transition, to have a non-ideal apparent Hill steepness so the pH-rate profile can broaden or sharpen asymmetrically with pH while retaining rapid equilibrium and the same substrate-dependent pKa shift framework.
response_change.observable_effect: At fixed S, the alkaline limb can fall off more gradually or more abruptly than the acidic limb, changing the width and asymmetry of the pH optimum; across S, the shift of the optimum remains but the flank curvature is no longer locked to the parent’s unit-log-slope form.

evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the mechanism appears as unequal acidic versus alkaline flank curvature at measured substrate levels; in holdout, the same non-ideal steepness persists while the existing substrate-dependent pKa shift moves where that curvature is expressed along the pH axis.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Set the new apparent steepness parameter to 1 to recover the parent law exactly.

evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because it changes the functional pH sensitivity of the alkaline loss process itself, altering local curvature and asymmetry rather than merely translating the optimum or rescaling the whole rate surface.

evolution_contract.assumption_after: The alkaline inactivation transition can have non-ideal apparent steepness while the acidic transition remains ideal.

evolution_contract.parent_reduction: Setting n_high = 1 recovers the parent expression exactly.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: With pH and S independently varied, the parent gives a bell-shaped activity surface whose alkaline flank curvature is fixed once the optimum position is set by pKa_high and the shared occupancy shift. The child preserves the same substrate-driven pKa translation but changes the alkaline-side steepness, so at fixed moderate or high S the rate can decay more sharply or more broadly on the alkaline side than any single parent parameter set can while keeping the same peak location and acidic flank.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: Refitting all existing parent parameters cannot reproduce this contrast across the stated conditions because pKa_high primarily shifts where alkaline decline occurs, k_cat and E_total rescale amplitude, K_M changes substrate saturation, and delta_pKa_coupling translates both pKa boundaries with occupancy. None changes the alkaline branch exponent independently of position, so one parent parameter set cannot match unequal acidic versus alkaline flank curvature over pH while also preserving the observed S-dependent optimum shifts.

Child change: relax the ideal-slope assumption for one existing protonation transition, giving a changed target mapping from inputs (pH,S) to rate through altered flank curvature, not merely an auxiliary reinterpretation. Admissible conditions: this matters only when pH sampling spans the flank and activity is above noise; if observations cluster near the peak or only on the acidic side, the refinement may be weakly identified.

change_summary: The single shared delta_pKa_coupling was replaced by flank-specific couplings delta_pKa_low and delta_pKa_high. This allows substrate concentration to widen, narrow, or skew the pH-activity window instead of only shifting both flanks together.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: A single shared delta_pKa_coupling applies identically to both the acidic activation transition and the alkaline inactivation transition.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Substrate binding can differentially stabilize distinct protonation microstates or conformations linked to the two macroscopic ionization steps, causing occupancy-dependent shifts of the low- and high-pH boundaries with different magnitudes.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The successor reduces to the parent when delta_pKa_low = delta_pKa_high.

response_change.parent_relation: The parent uses one shared substrate-dependent pKa shift, so increasing S translates both acidic and alkaline activity-loss boundaries together along the pH axis through the same saturation factor S/(K_M + S).

response_change.observable_effect: At low versus saturating S, the pH of half-maximal loss on the acidic flank and the pH of half-maximal loss on the alkaline flank move by unequal amounts, changing the peak location and width in a way the parent cannot match with one common coupling parameter.

activation_condition: Most visible when pH samples extend through and above the alkaline activity-loss flank and substrate occupancy varies appreciably from low to near-saturating values, i.e. S spanning values below and around K_M so theta changes substantially.
train_hidden_contrast: In training, varying pH at several substrate levels already reveals substrate-dependent movement of the active window; in holdout, the same mechanism predicts that the upper-flank curvature and apparent width also change with substrate rather than only translating rigidly.
continuation_path: Recover the parent when the alkaline non-ideality vanishes, e.g. the added high-pH steepness correction tends to zero and the effective alkaline Hill coefficient returns to the parent's constant n_high.

dependent_variable.description: Instantaneous substrate-conversion rate at the specified pH and substrate concentration

independent_variables.description: Bulk solution acidity on the pH scale
